title: Subway Stops
statement: A transit app finds the fewest stops between two of 400 stations joined by 600 tracks. Every stop counts the same.

approaches.name: Breadth-first search from the start station
approaches.hint: Spread out one ring at a time
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: The first time BFS reaches the target is along the fewest stops, and each station and track is handled once.

approaches.name: Depth-first search through every possible route, keeping the shortest
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but the number of routes grows explosively with the network.

approaches.name: Depth-first search, returning the first route found
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Fast, but the first route found is often far from the shortest.

approaches.name: Look up the answer in the adjacency matrix
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: The matrix only says whether two stations are directly joined, not how many stops apart they are.

title: Counting Lakes
statement: A satellite image is a 2,000 × 2,000 grid of water and land pixels. Count the lakes: groups of water pixels joined up, down, left or right.
examples: A grid with three separate water areas: 3

approaches.name: Scan the grid; at each unvisited water pixel, count one lake and mark its whole area with BFS
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Every pixel is marked once, so all the searches together cost one pass over the image. BFS avoids deep recursion on large lakes.

approaches.name: The same scan, marking each lake with recursive DFS
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Same count of work, but a lake of millions of pixels can make the recursion too deep for the call stack.

approaches.name: Start a new search from every water pixel without a shared visited mark
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Each lake is searched again from every one of its pixels and counted many times.

approaches.name: Count the water pixels
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: That gives the total area of water, not the number of separate lakes.

title: Power Grid Islands
statement: A utility has 100,000 substations and 150,000 cables (each cable joins two substations both ways). It needs the number of separate networks, so it knows how many control centres to staff.

approaches.name: Build an adjacency list, then run BFS or DFS from each unvisited substation and count the starts
approaches.hint: Each new start is a new network
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Every substation and cable is handled once, and substations with no cables are counted as networks of their own.

approaches.name: For every pair of substations, search whether they are connected
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: It can work out the groups, but billions of searches are far too slow.

approaches.name: Count the components found from the substations listed in the cables
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Substations with no cables never appear in the cable list, so they are missed.

approaches.name: Return V − E
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: That only holds when there are no cycles; one loop of cables makes it wrong.
